unlabelled.title: My Year On A Factory Floor Assembly Line

passages.text: When I was 19, I spent a year assembling electrical relays on a factory floor for $10/hr.
claims: The author spent a year assembling electrical relays on a factory floor at age 19 and was paid $10 per hour.

passages.text: I was pretty excited to get the job.
I’d been applying to much worse - I remember looking at at a craigslist ad for a sewage worker, which included a warning that it might be pretty gross.
claims: Before getting the relay-assembly job, the author applied for a sewage-worker job advertised on Craigslist that warned the work might be unpleasant.

passages.text: I applied for that too.
claims: The author applied for the Craigslist sewage-worker job.

passages.text: Knowingless is a reader-supported publication.
claims: Knowingless is a publication supported by its readers.

passages.text: To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
I really needed money.
I was so poor I going hungry, would scrape change off the street for meals.
claims: The author was so poor that they sometimes went hungry and collected coins from the street to pay for meals.

passages.text: I remember when touring a cheap room in northern Idaho to rent in a house full of strangers, they showed me the fridge, and I asked if people ever ate each other’s leftovers.
claims: While viewing an inexpensive room for rent in a house in northern Idaho, the author asked the residents whether they ate one another’s leftovers.

passages.text: They reassured me no, of course nobody would touch your food, and I was disappointed.
claims: The residents told the author that nobody would touch their food, and the author felt disappointed.

passages.text: That’s not what I had been trying to ask.
I’d grown up in a very isolated, borderline-cult type of world where my parents had made it clear that they’d give me no financial assistance once I left home.
claims: The author grew up in an isolated environment, and their parents told them they would not provide financial assistance after the author left home.

passages.text: Once you’re 18, you’re on your own, get a job, support yourself.
claims: The author's parents expected the author to become financially independent at age 18.

passages.text: It didn’t even occur to me to let them know I was going hungry; I just figured that’s what happened to people when you were an adult.
College wasn’t viable to me; I’d enrolled briefly but got kicked out after a few months once the finances didn’t work out.
claims: The author briefly enrolled in college but left after a few months when they could not make the finances work.

passages.text: A combination of my being homeschooled my entire life (weird transcripts), my parents making just too much money for me to qualify for financial aid while simultaneously refusing to cosign any loans at all, meant my path forward was not going to be one of education.
claims: The author was homeschooled throughout their childhood, did not qualify for financial aid because of their parents' income, and could not obtain parent-cosigned loans because their parents refused to cosign.

passages.text: So when Schweitzer Engineering Labs called to tell me I got the assembly line job at their Pullman manufacturing location, I was thrilled.
claims: Schweitzer Engineering Labs offered the author an assembly-line job at its Pullman manufacturing location, and the author was pleased.

passages.text: It paid a full ten dollars an hour (in 2011).
claims: The assembly-line job at Schweitzer Engineering Labs paid the author $10 per hour in 2011.

passages.text: My last job, shelving books at the Nampa public library, had been $7.25 an hour.
claims: Before the assembly-line job, the author shelved books at the Nampa public library for $7.25 per hour.

passages.text: And the assembly line job was indoors and I didn’t have to handle any poop!
claims: The assembly-line job was indoors and did not require the author to handle feces.

passages.text: Amazing.
They said to show up at ~7am for training.
claims: The employer instructed the author to arrive at approximately 7 a.m. for training.

passages.text: I’d thought jobs usually started at 8am, and was disappointed that it was so early.
But I was grateful to have a job at all, and I was an adult now and I knew being an adult was supposed to be very difficult, so I said ‘okay’ and showed up at 7.
claims: The author agreed to the employer's training schedule and arrived at 7 a.m.

passages.text: They put me and other new hires in a little room and we learned about the history of the company and how electrical relays worked and how the manufacturing floor functioned and then they showed us what all the tools were, how to screw and unscrew things, how to solder, etc.
claims: The employer trained the author and other new hires in a room, covering company history, electrical relays, factory operations, tools, fastening and unfastening, and soldering.

passages.text: I liked learning things and I had a great time.
I was determined to do awesome and I paid attention and tried super hard.
After a few days training was over, I passed their mini tests with flying colors, and they said great - show up tomorrow at 6:30am.
claims: After a few days of training, the author passed the employer's tests and was told to arrive at 6:30 a.m. the next day.

passages.text: I was oh wow.
That’s kinda early.
They were like oh yeah right my bad, actually you’re on mandatory overtime, work starts at 5:30am.
claims: The employer told the author that mandatory overtime meant work would start at 5:30 a.m.

passages.text: I shortly find out that it’s only sometimes 5:30; much of my time working there required us clocking in before 5am.
claims: During much of the author's time at the factory, employees were required to clock in before 5 a.m.

passages.text: Oh, and you have to work Saturdays.
claims: The author was required to work Saturdays at the factory.

passages.text: Sometimes if we’re really strapped, you need to come in on Sunday too.
claims: When the factory was short-staffed, the author sometimes had to work on Sundays.

passages.text: I lived 22 minutes away, so I spent my 19th year on this planet waking up at ~4:15am, getting home at 3:30pm, and going to sleep at 8pm, 6-7 days a week.
claims: While working at the factory at age 19, the author lived a 22-minute commute away, woke at about 4:15 a.m., returned home at 3:30 p.m., and went to bed at 8 p.m. six or seven days per week.

passages.text: I got assigned to a section near the end, where we put the relays into the metal boxes and wired then up.
claims: The author was assigned to a section near the end of the production line, where workers placed relays in metal boxes and wired them.

passages.text: Everything was on the same huge floor, the units just slowly flowed down the line and got shipped out the butt end of the building.
claims: The production process took place on one large factory floor, where units moved down a line and were shipped from the building.

passages.text: There were no windows visible to us.
claims: The factory workers in the author's area could not see any windows.

passages.text: When you arrive you get lockers where you put your stuff, and you have a little blue antistatic jacket/overcoat thing, and you put on special gloves and goggles and have to de-electrify yourself by plugging a wire from your coat into the wall.
claims: At the factory, workers used lockers and wore blue antistatic coats, gloves, and goggles, and grounded themselves by connecting a wire from their coats to a wall.

passages.text: Everything smelled SO specific, it’s hard to describe - like rubber and metal and other stuff I don’t have a term for.
I was determined to have a good time.
I believed happiness was a choice, and if I just worked hard enough and was good and tried that things would go okay.
I wanted to make everyone’s lives better, so I was annoyingly cheerful.
Just downright homeschool-levels of goofy.
The units got passed down the floor on trays and these rubber pads.
claims: At the factory, units moved along the floor on trays and rubber pads.

passages.text: When I had a little downtime (which was rare and inadvised, they told us strictly that you should be finding something to do nonstop.
claims: Downtime was rare and discouraged at the factory, where workers were instructed to stay continuously occupied.

passages.text: If you are waiting for another assembler to finish their unit to pass to you, you should start immediately cleaning), I would scratch little cartoons or messages or silly things into the rubber pads.
claims: The author sometimes scratched small cartoons, messages, or other marks into the rubber pads while waiting for another assembler to finish a unit.

passages.text: They were very superficial and hard to see, you had to just catch the light reflecting off of them at the right angle to notice, and if you rub it really hard it fades away.
claims: The author's marks on the rubber pads were faint, visible only at certain angles, and could be rubbed away.

passages.text: I did this for weeks.
claims: The author scratched marks into the rubber pads for several weeks.

passages.text: One day I came in and my team was in a special meeting, a rare huddle.
claims: One day, the author's team held an unusual special meeting.

passages.text: All the teams on the entire floor were in their own huddles.
claims: All the teams on the factory floor were gathered in separate meetings.

passages.text: They gravely told us that someone had been VANDALIZING the equipment, and that they needed to find out who it is and that terrible vandal will have to replace everything - many thousands of dollars.
claims: Factory management told the author's team that someone had damaged equipment, that management intended to identify the person responsible, and that the person might have to pay thousands of dollars to replace it.

passages.text: I was horrified and filled with shame.

The next day I went to a company computer and emailed someone as high up as I could find (I think possibly the CEO?) admitting it was me and I’m sorry and I don’t know how I’ll be able to pay for it but I can try somehow, maybe take it out of my wages.
claims: The day after the meeting, the author emailed a senior person at the company, admitted making the marks on the rubber pads, apologized, and offered to try to pay for the damage.

passages.text: I never heard back; probably it got caught in some filter meant to prevent the plebians from reaching the consuls.
claims: The author received no reply to the email they sent to a senior person at the company.

passages.text: I did this on a break.
claims: The author sent the email during a work break.

passages.text: We got two legally-mandated 15 minute breaks (in addition to lunch).
claims: The author's workplace provided two 15-minute breaks in addition to lunch, which the author describes as legally mandated.

passages.text: It was a big floor, and took a few minutes to walk into the break room, so the actual breaks were closer to like 9 minutes.
claims: The walk across the factory floor to the break room took several minutes, reducing the author's effective break time to about nine minutes.

passages.text: The lunches were generous; we got a full 45 minutes or hour, I forget.
claims: The author's lunch break lasted either 45 minutes or an hour.

passages.text: They gave us free lunches on Fridays, where the entire company piled into the big special lunch room and we got some kind of presentation.
claims: The company provided free Friday lunches, during which employees gathered in a large lunchroom for a presentation.

passages.text: There I got to see the other people who worked at the factory - not the assemblers, but the engineers, and the managers, and marketers, and whoever else.
claims: At the Friday lunches, the author saw factory employees including engineers, managers, and marketers.

passages.text: I’d watch them longingly.
I really wanted to be one of those.
I had this idea that if I just worked really hard and really well on the factory floor, that eventually I could become one of them.
I had some vague belief that I had a lot of potential.
I was vibrating with vision and an overactive mind.
I thought I can do what they do but I have no idea how to get there.
Eventually I figured out this wasn’t how it worked.
The company advertised some educational program for assemblers to turn into brain people, but I couldn’t afford it.
claims: The company advertised an educational program intended to help assemblers qualify for other kinds of work, but the author could not afford it.

passages.text: I kept meeting coworkers who’d been on the assembly line floor for decades.
claims: The author met coworkers who had worked on the assembly line for decades.

passages.text: After many months I finally get pulled into a manager’s office for a performance review and they give me a 25 cent raise.
claims: After working at the factory for many months, the author received a performance review and a 25-cent raise.

passages.text: I slowly lost hope.
I really tried to hold on, but exhaustion made my fingers start slipping.
I was tired all the time.
I got a friend to buy me some alcohol (19 years old remember) and started drinking many nights, which led to me being hungover and nonfunctional during the work hours.
claims: At age 19, the author had a friend buy alcohol for them and began drinking on many nights, which left them hungover and unable to function well at work.

passages.text: I hateed the work.
It was a horrible no-good kind of work.
You couldn’t zone out and just do autopilot, because you had to follow a set of instructions with slight variations, that change a little each time.
claims: The author's assembly work required following instructions that varied slightly from task to task, making it difficult to work on autopilot.

passages.text: You had to pay attention.
claims: The assembly work required the author to pay attention.

passages.text: But the attention you paid was not interesting; it was ongoing, it was relentless, it was stupid.
My mind wasn’t mine, it was just barely pulled over some threshhold into a mind-killing, mundane amount of repetition.
I was bad at it.
Before this I’d tended to be naturally good at almost everything I tried.
I learned very fast.
But here I made more mistakes than almost anyone else.
claims: The author made more mistakes on the assembly line than nearly all of their coworkers.

passages.text: They tracked mistakes; people spot-checked your work, and you got an anonymized code and you could go look at a leaderboard to see where your code ranked among others.
claims: The factory tracked assembly errors through spot checks and assigned workers anonymous codes that they could use to view their rankings on a leaderboard.

passages.text: This depressed me more; how would I climb through the ranks and become an engineer if I accidentally screwed the blue wire onto the wrong node once every 200 times?
They didn’t want us to sit, and I think I started working there at the end of some kind of sitting war, because there were a few scattered chairs and angry muttering longtimers.
claims: Factory management discouraged workers from sitting, although a few chairs were available when the author began working there.

passages.text: Management thought sitting was bad and would destroy productivity, but some of the assemblers had fought back with cries of back pain, so they’d grudgingly allowed us a small number of chairs.
claims: Management believed that sitting would reduce productivity, but allowed a limited number of chairs after assemblers complained of back pain.

passages.text: I was young, so did not get first access to a chair, but I loved it when I did.
It made my day so so much better.
Standing hurt, and made me worse at everything, and made me tired and sad.
After a few months I got moved up the line, to the section where they installed the boards into the units.
claims: After a few months, the author was reassigned to a section of the production line where workers installed boards into units.

passages.text: This was less physically intensive, but more mentally draining.
We assembled lots of different types of units, and the units went through different corresponding flow lines that had the required amount of tools.
claims: The factory assembled multiple types of units, which used different production lines equipped with the tools needed for each.

passages.text: But they wouldn’t let you sit and learn a single line, which might have one day allowed you to get used to it enough to zone out and have thoughts that were your own.
claims: The author says workers were not permitted to remain at one production line long enough to become fully familiar with it.

passages.text: No - you had to rotate spots regularly, so that you were always just slightly unfamiliar with your current task.
claims: Factory workers had to rotate workstations regularly and were consequently often unfamiliar with their current tasks.

passages.text: They did this so if people were out sick or something they could flexibly fill the gap, but it resulted in everyone being slightly worse at everything.
claims: The employer rotated workers among tasks to cover absences, and the author believed this made workers less proficient at each task.

passages.text: There was no groove to fall into.
It was an infinite series of tiny tasks that changed a little bit all the time, and a lot sometimes, and if you fail someone might DIE.
claims: The author's work involved frequently changing assembly tasks, and the author believed that an assembly error could potentially cause someone's death.

passages.text: And then randomly you’d get thrown into the picker role, which meant you spent the day working in the warehouse.
claims: The author was sometimes assigned to a picker role in the warehouse for a day.

passages.text: You’d have to haul in a big stacked tray on wheels and go down a list of paper and then run around the shelves pulling boxes off and scanning them and hauling the tray back.
claims: The picker role involved using a wheeled tray, following a paper list, retrieving and scanning boxes from shelves, and returning the tray.

passages.text: This was awesome cause it meant at least you weren’t standing still, but it was physically exhausting and happened rarely enough you never got used to it.
Throughout it all, I was still grateful.
I saved most of my money, and felt like a king sitting on a savings account of a few thousand dollars.
claims: The author saved most of their earnings and accumulated a few thousand dollars.

passages.text: I was happy I was not working in poop.
I was happy to not be hungry.
But even so, the depression slowly crept around me and I had this sense that I did not want to spend the rest of my life like this.
I was so confused by the coworkers that had been there for a decade+ and seemed content with their lives.
I thought we were all on a ship that had rescued us from the void and we were so thankful and just waiting for the ship to deliver us to better lands, and so why were you still on the boat?
Why had you not gotten off?
They were all poor.
claims: The author's coworkers were all poor.

passages.text: I had a few coworkers my age; one had come from a farm, the other wanted to do college but hadn’t managed to make it for some reason.
claims: The author had two coworkers of similar age; one came from a farm, and the other wanted to attend college but had not done so.

passages.text: Some were divorced moms, others jolly church guys.
claims: Some of the author's coworkers were divorced mothers, while others were men associated with a church whom the author considered jolly.

passages.text: We all shopped at wal-mart and used coupons for groceries.
claims: The author and their coworkers shopped at Walmart and used grocery coupons.

passages.text: I wondered about their lives outside of this, but there probably wasn’t actually that much life outside of this.
We were with each other for the majority of our waking hours.
claims: The author and their coworkers spent most of their waking hours together.

passages.text: The factory walled us in both in space and time.
I started calling in sick more often.
claims: The author began calling in sick more frequently.

passages.text: Sometimes I’d wake up and stare at the ceiling and just completely lack the will to make myself get up and go to work.
I started bumping up against management who frowned at me for taking so many days off.
claims: The author began having difficulties with management, who disapproved of the number of days the author took off.

passages.text: My compulsive please-authority streak was not strong enough to force me out of bed, often hungover, into yet another 9-10.5 hours under flourescent lights on a Saturday.
claims: The author sometimes missed Saturday shifts that lasted 9 to 10.5 hours, despite feeling pressure to comply with authority, and was often hungover.

passages.text: I got out because I got another job.
claims: The speaker left their previous job because they got another job.

passages.text: I’d been watching other job ads on craigslist and saw one opening for a boudoir photographer.
claims: The speaker had been looking at job advertisements on Craigslist and saw an opening for a boudoir photographer.

passages.text: I liked taking photos of my pretty friends on weekends, and  so I applied, and showed them all the pretty photos I’d taken, and one day after work when I was in a hardware store they called me to tell me I was hired.
claims: The speaker enjoyed taking photos of friends on weekends, applied for a boudoir photographer job, showed the employer their photos, and was told they had been hired while at a hardware store after work.

passages.text: I almost died of joy.
I told everyone at the assembly line I was getting out, and they were so happy for me.
claims: The speaker told their assembly-line coworkers they were leaving, and the coworkers were happy for the speaker.

passages.text: I remember my last day clearing out my locker and walking out for the very last time and they were congratulating me and wishing me luck and then I was gone.
claims: On the speaker’s last day at the assembly-line job, they cleared out their locker and left, while coworkers congratulated them and wished them luck.

passages.text: I went to the clothing store and asked the lady working there to suggest office clothes for me, because I was going to be a professional now.
claims: The speaker went to a clothing store, asked an employee to suggest office clothes, and intended to work as a professional.

passages.text: She handed me a set of clothes and I bought them all.
claims: A clothing-store employee handed the speaker a set of clothes, and the speaker bought all of them.

passages.text: No more blue antistatic factory coat!
claims: The speaker no longer had to wear a blue antistatic coat at the factory.

passages.text: The photography job lasted two weeks.
claims: The speaker’s photography job lasted two weeks.

passages.text: I’d just turned 20 and I’d been homeschooled my whole life and I had no idea how to interact with people where I was in a role of authority.
claims: When the speaker started the photography job, they had recently turned 20, had been homeschooled throughout their life, and felt they did not know how to interact with people while in an authority role.

passages.text: I’d had all fire quite literally beaten out of me and was compulsively submissive, quiet, nervous.
I was not good at making strangers feel sexy and like I had everything under control in photoshoots.
claims: The speaker was not skilled at making strangers feel sexy and feel that the speaker was in control during photoshoots.

passages.text: The boss called me into his office and said sorry, we need to let you go.
claims: The speaker’s boss called them into his office and told them they were being let go.

passages.text: I said okay.
claims: The speaker responded to being told they were being let go by saying okay.

passages.text: I understand.
claims: The speaker told their boss that they understood they were being let go.

passages.text: I walked out, wearing my ill-fitting ‘office’ clothes I’d bought for this job, climbed into my beat-up little car, and wailed like death the entire drive home.
claims: After being let go, the speaker left wearing the office clothes they had bought for the job, got into their car, and cried loudly throughout the drive home.

passages.text: This was my one shot out into a better life and I’d blown it.
I had no idea what I was going to do, but I knew no matter what happened, I would not return to the ship that had rescued me from the void.

I had a little bit of savings to sustain me for some months, and so I began trying and failing, trying and failing, over and over again, until one day I met a man off okcupid who asked if I’d ever heard of this thing called webcamming.
claims: After losing the photography job, the speaker had enough savings to support them for several months, repeatedly tried and failed at unspecified efforts, and eventually met a man on OkCupid who asked whether they had heard of webcamming.

passages.text: Most of the nightmares I ever have are about the factory floor.
I dream I have to go back for some reason, I’ve lost my job, I have to go recover something and they need my help and I get sucked in.
It’s strange for that place to be such a nightmare for me -
so many other people are working there, right now as you read this, and presumably they do not feel like they’re in a nightmare.
claims: At the time the passage was written, other people were working at the factory, and the speaker assumes they did not experience the workplace as a nightmare.

passages.text: Maybe they’re good at their jobs.
claims: The speaker suggests that some of the factory workers may be good at their jobs.

passages.text: They get decent health insurance and plenty of money for groceries and a free lunch every Friday.
claims: The factory workers receive health insurance the speaker considers decent, enough money for groceries, and a free lunch every Friday.

passages.text: Am I weak, for failing to endure what others can thrive on?
Is something in me so brittle I had to drink to coat my exposed nerves?
I don’t know.
But I think about them a lot, and I hope one day we can get a nicer, bigger boat to rescue them again.
